blocks.title: Mass spectrometry
blocks.md:
In the mass spectrometer a molecule loses an electron to give the **molecular ion M⁺**; its m/z gives the relative molecular mass. M⁺ breaks into **fragments** whose peaks reveal the structure (m/z 15 CH₃⁺, 29 C₂H₅⁺, 43 C₃H₇⁺ or CH₃CO⁺, 45 COOH⁺, 77 C₆H₅⁺). Compounds with **Br** show M and M+2 peaks of equal height (⁷⁹Br : ⁸¹Br about 1 : 1); with **Cl** about 3 : 1.

The **M+1 peak** (due to ¹³C, 1.1 % abundance) gives the number of carbons: n ≈ (height of M+1 ÷ height of M) × 100/1.1.

blocks.title: Infrared absorption (wavenumber / cm⁻¹)
blocks.md:
A bond absorbs IR when its vibration changes the dipole. Characteristic ranges: **O–H** (alcohol) 3200–3550 broad; **O–H** (carboxylic acid) 2500–3300 very broad; **N–H** 3300–3500; **C–H** 2850–3100; **C≡N** 2200–2260; **C=O** 1680–1750 (strong, sharp); **C=C** 1620–1680; **C–O** 1000–1300. The region below about 1500 cm⁻¹ is the **fingerprint region**, unique to each compound.

Example: a strong band near 1715 cm⁻¹ and no broad O–H means a ketone or aldehyde.

blocks.caption: Schematic ¹H NMR spectrum of ethyl ethanoate: a triplet (CH₃), a singlet (CH₃CO) and a quartet (OCH₂).
blocks.alt: A schematic NMR spectrum with a triplet near 1.2 ppm, a singlet near 2.0 ppm and a quartet near 4.1 ppm.

blocks.title: ¹H NMR
blocks.md: Protons in different chemical environments give separate signals. **Number of signals** = number of environments; **chemical shift** δ (ppm, from TMS = 0): alkyl C–H 0.9–1.5; next to C=O 2.0–2.7; O–CH₂ 3.3–4.3; alkene 4.5–6.5; aromatic 6.5–8.0; aldehyde 9–10; carboxylic acid 10–12. **Integration** gives the ratio of H atoms. **Splitting**: a signal is split into (n + 1) lines by n protons on the adjacent carbons (singlet, doublet, triplet 1:2:1, quartet 1:3:3:1). OH and NH signals vanish on shaking with D₂O.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Reading M+2 for chlorine and bromine the wrong way round (Br 1 : 1, Cl 3 : 1).
- Counting H atoms from the signal height instead of the integration.
- Confusing C=O (about 1700 cm⁻¹) and C=C (about 1650 cm⁻¹).
- Forgetting that equivalent protons do not split each other (for example CH₃–CH₂– gives a triplet and a quartet, each split only by the neighbour).

blocks.title: Example 1 — Deducing a structure
blocks.statement: A compound C₄H₈O₂ has a strong IR absorption at 1740 cm⁻¹ and no broad band above 2500 cm⁻¹. Its ¹H NMR has three signals: δ 1.2 (triplet, 3H), δ 2.0 (singlet, 3H), δ 4.1 (quartet, 2H). Identify it.
steps: Degree of unsaturation = (2 × 4 + 2 − 8)/2 = 1. The strong band at 1740 cm⁻¹ shows C=O; no broad O–H means it is not an acid: an ester.
δ 4.1 quartet (2H) = O–CH₂ next to CH₃; δ 1.2 triplet (3H) = the CH₃ of the ethyl group; δ 2.0 singlet (3H) = CH₃ next to C=O with no neighbours.
The compound is CH₃COOCH₂CH₃, ethyl ethanoate.

blocks.title: Example 2 — Mass spectrum
blocks.statement: A compound shows peaks at m/z 108 and 110 of equal height, and a fragment at m/z 29. Identify it.
steps: Equal M and M+2 peaks indicate one bromine atom (⁷⁹Br and ⁸¹Br).

blocks.title: The Haber process
blocks.md: N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g), ΔH = −92 kJ mol⁻¹. Conditions: iron catalyst, about **400–450 °C**, **150–250 atm**. A low temperature would give a better yield (exothermic) but too slow a rate; a high pressure favours fewer gas moles (4 → 2) but is expensive: so a **compromise**. The ammonia is condensed to a liquid and the unreacted gases are **recycled**. Ammonia is used to make fertilisers (ammonium nitrate, ammonium sulfate, urea), nitric acid and explosives.

blocks.title: The Contact process
blocks.md: S → SO₂ (burning sulfur or roasting sulfide ores), then **2SO₂ + O₂ ⇌ 2SO₃** (ΔH = −196 kJ mol⁻¹) with a **V₂O₅ catalyst**, about 450 °C and 1–2 atm (the yield is already high at this pressure, so a high pressure is not worth the cost). SO₃ is absorbed in concentrated H₂SO₄ to make oleum (H₂S₂O₇), which is diluted with water; SO₃ is not dissolved directly in water (a mist forms). Uses: fertilisers, detergents, batteries, paints, ore processing.

blocks.caption: Flow diagram of the Haber process with recycling of unreacted gases.
blocks.alt: Boxes for the nitrogen–hydrogen feed, compressor, reactor, condenser and liquid ammonia with a recycle line back to the feed.

blocks.title: Calculations and green chemistry
blocks.md:
**Percentage yield** = actual/theoretical × 100. **Atom economy** = (M of desired product ÷ sum of M of all products, or reactants) × 100: higher is better. **Percentage N** in a fertiliser = (mass of N ÷ M) × 100: urea 46.7 %, NH₄NO₃ 35 %, (NH₄)₂SO₄ 21 %.

Principles: use catalysts, recycle unreacted materials, reduce waste and energy, use renewable feedstocks.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Saying the best conditions are those giving the highest yield: cost, rate and safety matter too.
- Claiming a catalyst increases the yield of a reversible reaction.
- Forgetting to recycle unreacted gases when describing the Haber process.
- Mixing up acid rain (SO₂, NOₓ) with the greenhouse effect (CO₂, CH₄) and ozone depletion (CFCs).

blocks.title: Environmental chemistry
blocks.md:
- **Acid rain**: SO₂ (from burning sulfur-containing fuels) and NOₓ dissolve in water to give H₂SO₄ and HNO₃; damages buildings, forests and lakes.
- **Greenhouse effect**: CO₂, CH₄ and water vapour absorb infrared radiation; more CO₂ increases global temperature.
- **Ozone depletion**: Cl• from CFCs catalyses the breakdown of ozone: Cl• + O₃ → ClO• + O₂.
- **Eutrophication**: excess nitrate and phosphate (fertilisers) causes algal blooms that deplete oxygen in water.

blocks.title: Example 1 — Ammonia and fertilisers
blocks.statement: How much ammonia can be made from 1.00 tonne of nitrogen at 100 % yield? What mass of urea, CO(NH₂)₂ (M = 60), supplies 25.0 kg of nitrogen to a field?
steps: N₂ → 2NH₃: 28 g N₂ gives 34 g NH₃, so 1.00 t gives 34/28 = 1.21 t.
Percentage N in urea = 28/60 × 100 = 46.7 % (two N atoms).
Mass of urea for 25.0 kg N = 25.0/0.467 = 53.6 kg.
blocks.answer: 1.21 t of ammonia; 53.6 kg of urea

blocks.title: Example 2 — Conversion and atom economy
blocks.statement: In a Haber reactor 1.0 mol N₂ and 3.0 mol H₂ react until 20 % of the N₂ has reacted. Find the mole fraction of NH₃. Calculate the atom economy of making ethanol by fermentation: C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2C₂H₅OH + 2CO₂.
steps: N₂ left 0.80 mol, H₂ left 2.40 mol, NH₃ formed 0.40 mol; total = 3.60 mol; mole fraction of NH₃ = 0.40/3.60 = 0.111.
Hydration of ethene (C₂H₄ + H₂O → C₂H₅OH) has an atom economy of 100 %.

blocks.title: Titration technique and uncertainty
blocks.md: Rinse the pipette with the solution it will deliver and the burette with its own solution; use a white tile; swirl; add dropwise near the end-point; read at the bottom of the meniscus at eye level; repeat until **concordant titres** (within 0.10 cm³). Uncertainty: the burette has an uncertainty of ±0.05 cm³ for each reading, so a titre (two readings) has **±0.10 cm³**; a 25.00 cm³ pipette ±0.06 cm³ (typical). **Percentage uncertainty** = (absolute ÷ measured value) × 100; add the percentages of all measurements used in a quotient/product.

blocks.title: Planning and evaluation
blocks.md: State the independent, dependent and control variables; choose apparatus with suitable precision; give quantities and a method for **safety** (dilute acids, fume cupboards for chlorine/ammonia); predict the shape of the results. To evaluate: identify the largest percentage uncertainty (it limits the accuracy), distinguish systematic (zero errors, wrong indicator) from random errors, and suggest improvements (larger titres, a more precise balance, repeats).

white ppt, dissolves in excess NaOH

blocks.caption: Test results for some cations with sodium hydroxide solution.
blocks.alt: Five labelled rows listing ions Cu2+, Fe2+, Fe3+, Al3+ and NH4+ with the colour of the precipitate or the observation.

blocks.title: Qualitative tests
blocks.md: **Gases**: H₂ burns with a squeaky pop; O₂ relights a glowing splint; CO₂ turns limewater milky; NH₃ turns damp red litmus blue; Cl₂ bleaches damp litmus; SO₂ turns acidified dichromate from orange to green. **Anions**: carbonate (dilute acid → CO₂); sulfate (acidified BaCl₂ → white precipitate); halides (acidified AgNO₃ → white/cream/yellow). **Cations**: NaOH(aq) and NH₃(aq) as in the figure; ammonium ions: warm with NaOH, NH₃ released; flame tests for Group 1 and 2 metals.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Using a measuring cylinder instead of a pipette for the accurate volume.
- Including the first rough titre in the mean.
- Rinsing the conical flask with the solution it will contain (the pipette should be rinsed, not the flask).
- Reporting only 'a precipitate' without its colour, and writing 'turns the splint on' instead of 'relights a glowing splint'.

blocks.title: Example 1 — Percentage uncertainty
blocks.statement: A 25.00 cm³ pipette (±0.06 cm³) delivers acid, and the burette titre is 20.00 cm³ (two readings, each ±0.05 cm³). The concentration is 0.0800 mol dm⁻³. Find the percentage uncertainty in the concentration and the absolute uncertainty.
steps: Total percentage uncertainty = 0.24 + 0.50 = 0.74 % (the concentration depends on both volumes).
Absolute uncertainty = 0.74 % of 0.0800 = 0.0006 mol dm⁻³, so c = (0.0800 ± 0.0006) mol dm⁻³.

blocks.title: Example 2 — Identifying an unknown
blocks.statement: Solid X dissolves in water. With NaOH(aq) it gives a green precipitate that turns brown on standing; with acidified BaCl₂ it gives a white precipitate. Identify X.
steps: Green precipitate turning brown: Fe(OH)₂ oxidised in air to Fe(OH)₃, so the cation is Fe²⁺.
White precipitate with acidified BaCl₂: sulfate ions (BaSO₄).
